interviewQuestions.question: You can't measure live accuracy in real time — how do you monitor the model anyway?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd first name why this happens: the true label often arrives long after the prediction — a loan-default label might not be known for a year, a fraud label depends on a dispute process that takes weeks — so an accuracy-only monitoring plan is always looking backward at stale information, or sometimes never gets a signal at all. Instead, I'd build monitoring in layers that don't require labels. First, **input feature distribution monitoring** — track each feature's statistics (mean, variance, or a distributional distance like population stability index) against the training distribution, computable the instant a request arrives; a sudden shift is an early warning that the world has changed. Second, **prediction distribution monitoring** — track the model's own output distribution over time; if a fraud model that normally flags 2% of transactions jumps to 15% flagged, that's a signal regardless of whether I know the true fraud rate yet. Third, once labels do eventually arrive (even delayed), I'd close the loop with actual accuracy as a lagging confirmation, and I'd track the label arrival lag itself as its own metric. I'd set alerting thresholds on the first two layers specifically because they're my only real-time signal, and I'd pair this with a retraining trigger — either scheduled or drift-triggered — so a detected shift actually leads to action, not just a dashboard nobody looks at.

**Testing:** whether you understand that feature/prediction distribution monitoring exist specifically because labels are delayed, not as a lesser substitute for accuracy but as the genuinely available real-time signal.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Label-free monitoring layers

interviewQuestions.question: What's the practical difference between data drift and concept drift, and why does misdiagnosing which one you're facing lead to the wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Data drift is a shift in the input feature distribution while the true relationship between features and the target stays the same — a fraud model suddenly sees more transactions from a newly launched country, but what actually makes a transaction fraudulent hasn't changed at all, just the mix of inputs the model now sees. Concept drift is the deeper problem: the relationship itself between features and target changes — fraudsters adopt a genuinely new tactic, so a feature pattern that used to reliably indicate legitimate behavior now indicates fraud, meaning the old learned mapping from features to outcome is now actively wrong, not just applied to an unfamiliar input mix.

The fix differs sharply between the two, which is why the diagnosis matters. Data drift can sometimes be handled without retraining at all — better feature coverage, re-weighting the training distribution to better match the new input mix, or simply verifying the model still generalizes fine to the new region of input space it wasn't well-represented in before. Concept drift cannot be fixed this way, because the model's learned parameters encode a relationship that's now genuinely stale — no amount of re-weighting old data helps, since the *old labels themselves* no longer describe current reality. Concept drift requires retraining on fresh labeled data that reflects the new relationship.

Misdiagnosing concept drift as data drift and responding with re-weighting or feature coverage fixes leaves the actual problem — a model applying an outdated rule — completely unaddressed, while the team believes they've responded to the alert. The practical tell: check whether the model's *error pattern* concentrates on inputs that are otherwise familiar (points toward concept drift, since it's not an unfamiliar-input problem) versus genuinely novel input regions (points toward data drift).

**Testing:** whether you can distinguish the two by mechanism, not just definition, and connect the distinction to why the wrong response fails to fix the real problem.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Data drift vs concept drift, and why the fix differs

interviewQuestions.question: Your feature-distribution monitoring has been flagging drift alerts for weeks, but the model's downstream business metrics look completely stable. Do you retrain, and how do you reason about this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't retrain automatically off the feature-drift alert alone — this is exactly the scenario where the monitoring layers exist specifically to disagree with each other, and that disagreement is informative rather than a bug to paper over. Feature-distribution monitoring is the earliest, cheapest, most sensitive signal precisely because it fires the instant an input distribution shifts at all, with no requirement that the shift actually matters to the model's predictions or the business outcome — it's designed to catch changes early, which structurally means it will also catch changes that turn out to be harmless. Downstream business metrics are the slowest, most lagging signal, but they're the ultimate ground truth for whether anything the model does actually matters to the outcome it exists to serve.

A stable business metric despite ongoing feature drift is a real, meaningful data point: it suggests either the specific features drifting aren't the ones the model relies on heavily for its actual predictions, or the model happens to be robust to this particular kind of input shift — both plausible and worth confirming rather than dismissing. My next step would be to check prediction-distribution monitoring as the middle layer: has the model's own output distribution shifted at all in response to the drifting features? If predictions are also stable, that's a coherent picture — feature drift that hasn't propagated into anything that matters yet — and I'd deprioritize an urgent retrain while keeping monitoring active, since drift can still worsen or eventually reach a feature that does matter.

What I'd explicitly avoid is either extreme: reflexively retraining on every feature-drift alert regardless of downstream impact (wasteful, and risks introducing regressions from an unnecessary retrain), or ignoring persistent alerts indefinitely just because nothing's broken yet, since drift that's currently harmless can still be an early sign of a larger shift still in progress.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the different sensitivities of the three monitoring layers together, rather than treating any single layer's alert as an automatic retraining trigger.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Reconciling drift alerts against stable business metrics
